privateCloud.title: Private Cloud (Nextcloud)
privateCloud.subtitle: Your company cloud on your own server — better data privacy and no monthly SaaS fees.
privateCloud.heroTitle: A private Nextcloud cloud on your server, without a SaaS subscription
privateCloud.heroSubtitle: I deploy a company cloud on your infrastructure: files, team access, and backups stay with you — not with a vendor in California.
privateCloud.feature1: Nextcloud installation and configuration on your infrastructure
privateCloud.feature3: Lower long-term cost by removing recurring subscription fees

whoFor.title: Who is a private Nextcloud cloud for?
whoFor.intro: I deploy Nextcloud for companies that want files and collaboration without a monthly tribute and without handing data to a US SaaS.

item1.title: A team that lives in files
item1.text: Law firms, agencies, workshops, project teams — anywhere Dropbox and Google Drive feel "good enough" until you count the subscription and the risk.

item2.title: Data you do not want to hand over
item2.text: Contracts, client files, photos, backups. If GDPR is not an empty slogan, the server should be yours, not "somewhere in the cloud".

item3.title: Poznań and Warsaw
item3.text: Install on a VPS, a dedicated box, or a machine in the office — in Poznań, in Warsaw, or wherever the server already stands. You do not need an IT department to stop renting Google Drive.

problem.title: Why Google Drive and Dropbox stop being convenient
problem.p1: The bill grows with the team. Files sit on someone else's servers, under someone else's jurisdiction. Leaving hurts, because nobody planned an exit when they clicked "14 days free".
problem.p2: A private cloud is not a hobby Nextcloud on a Raspberry Pi. It is your infrastructure: accounts, rules, backups — without a fee for every extra terabyte and without asking a vendor for permission to leave.

process.title: How a private-cloud deployment actually works
process.subtitle: No "cloud migration" slide deck. A machine, an install, the team, documentation.

step1.title: Conversation
step1.description: What you use today, how many people, which files, where the server should live. We decide whether a VPS, a dedicated box, or office hardware makes sense — I do not force a server on you.

step2.title: Infrastructure
step2.description: Address, certificate, disks, access. You see the plan before I install anything. No surprise "and here is another licence".

step3.title: Implementation
step3.description: Nextcloud, accounts, groups, backups, solid baseline security. Status updates along the way — not silence and not kickoff percentages.

step4.title: Handover
step4.description: Documentation for you and the team. 30 days of care after go-live, so I carry the risk that "the cloud does not boot on Monday", not your accountant.

includesMore.title: What else is included in the Nextcloud rollout?
includesMore.item1: Install on your machine — data does not leave for someone else's cloud "because it is easier".
includesMore.item2: Accounts, groups, and team access under your address, not under drive.google.com.
includesMore.item3: Backups and a hard security baseline, not a next-next-finish wizard.
includesMore.item4: A guide so the admin is not the only person who "knows the root password".
includesMore.item5: Code and data stay on your side. Nextcloud is open source — you are not renting your cloud.

whyCustom.title: Why not stay on Google Workspace?
whyCustom.p1: Workspace is convenient until you count five tools, five contracts, and the fact that your files live under a jurisdiction you did not choose. That is vendor lock-in for the office.
whyCustom.p2: Nextcloud is not a cheaper Google Drive. It is a decision: data stays with you, the software is open, and leaving does not require the vendor's permission. Digital sovereignty starts with files, not with a manifesto.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions about a private Nextcloud cloud
faq.subtitle: Straight answers before we book a call.

q1.question: How much does a private Nextcloud cloud cost?
q1.answer: The package starts at 5500 PLN net. That covers install, configuration, and handover — not a monthly fee forever. The server (a VPS or your hardware) is billed separately, because it should be yours, not mine.

q2.question: Does a private cloud help with GDPR?
q2.answer: Data sits on infrastructure you name — including an EU server if that is the choice. This does not replace a GDPR policy or processor agreements with your clients. It does reduce the usual problem: company files on servers whose location you do not control.

q3.question: Will I be able to use Nextcloud after handover?
q3.answer: Yes. You get a guide and a setup that feels like Drive — only under your address. Adding users, folders, and shares does not require a ticket to an agency. Updates and harder topics stay with care or with your admin.

q4.question: What about backups?
q4.answer: Backup is part of the configuration. A cloud without copies is just a nicer way to lose files. We decide where the copy lands and how often — before you put client contracts in it.

q5.question: How is this different from Synology, a NAS, or OwnCloud?
q5.answer: A NAS can be a good office disk and a weak remote setup. OwnCloud is a different product and path. I deploy Nextcloud as a company cloud: browser, phone, permissions, backups. If Synology already does the job, I will not sell a migration for sport.

q6.question: Do you issue a VAT invoice?
q6.answer: Yes. I operate legally in Poland, I issue an invoice, and you can deduct VAT. A conversation is not a contract — first we check whether we are a good fit.

website.title: Website
website.offerSubtitle: For experts building a personal brand and companies that want to be visible online.
website.heroTitle: A website that builds trust and sells
website.heroSubtitle: I design and implement websites that clearly communicate your brand's value and guide users to action.

whoFor.title: Who is this website for?
whoFor.intro: I build websites for experts, specialists, and companies that want to show up in Google and earn trust from the first click — not just "have a site".

item1.title: Personal brand
item1.text: Coaches, advisors, doctors, lawyers, trainers — people whose name should sell, and who need a professional website instead of a digital business card.

item2.title: Service business
item2.text: When a calling-card page is not enough and you need a website that explains the offer, answers doubts, and collects enquiries.

item3.title: Poznań and Warsaw
item3.text: I am based in Poznań. With Warsaw clients I work remotely and meet in person when I am in the city. You do not need a separate local agency.

problem.title: Why a simple calling-card site is not enough
problem.p1: Most websites look fine and sell nothing. A visitor arrives, does not understand the offer in five seconds, and goes back to Google. That is not a traffic problem. It is a decision problem.
problem.p2: A good website does three things: it says who you are, answers doubts, and leads to a conversation. The rest — animations, sliders, stock smiles — is decoration.

process.title: How a website project actually works
process.subtitle: No agency theatre. A conversation, a plan, implementation, handover.

step1.title: Conversation
step1.description: 15–30 minutes. We define the goal of the site, the audience, and what should happen after the click — contact, signup, or a booked call.

step2.title: Design and copy
step2.description: Layout, wording, and search-friendly structure. You see the direction before I write a line of code. No surprise at the end.

step3.title: Implementation
step3.description: Code, mobile version, form, basic SEO. You get regular status updates — not silence and not progress-bar slides.

step4.title: Handover
step4.description: Your website, your domain, a how-to guide. 30 days of technical care after launch, so I carry the failure risk, not you.

includesMore.title: What else is included in the website?
includesMore.item1: A responsive layout — the site works on a phone, not only on a laptop.
includesMore.item2: A contact form and a clear path to a conversation, not just a pretty header.
includesMore.item3: Meta titles, descriptions, and a sitemap so Google can actually find you.
includesMore.item4: A guide so you can add content yourself — blog posts, case studies, news.
includesMore.item5: Domain and hosting stay on your side. You are not locked into a website builder.

whyCustom.title: Why not Wix, a builder, or a "website for 300 zł"?
whyCustom.p1: A builder is fast until you want to change the rules. Then you pay a subscription, you do not own the code, and leaving hurts. That is vendor lock-in for a calling card.
whyCustom.p2: With me you get a website you actually own. Persuasion psychology in the layout, technical SEO in the background, and code you can take with you. You are not renting your presence online.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions about websites
faq.subtitle: Straight answers before we book a call.

q1.question: How much does a professional website cost?
q1.answer: The website package starts at 3500 PLN net. An expert calling-card site is a different job than a multi-page site with a blog — after a conversation you get a quote, not empty from-to ranges.

q2.question: Who is a personal-brand website for?
q2.answer: For people who sell competence: experts, specialists, service firms. If a client will Google you first, the website is your ZMOT — the moment you either earn trust or drop out.

q3.question: Will I be able to manage the website after launch?
q3.answer: Yes. You get a guide and a setup you can handle without being a developer. Adding a post, changing copy, or updating the offer does not require a ticket to an agency.

q4.question: How long does it take to build a website?
q4.answer: A straightforward expert site is usually a few weeks from kickoff to launch. The timeline depends on how fast we have copy, photos, and decisions — not on how many slides I show at a kickoff.

q5.question: Will the website show up in Google?
q5.answer: I prepare the technical layer: indexing, meta tags, sitemap, mobile version. Google has to be able to find and understand the site. Rankings for competitive terms are built with content, links, and time — which is why technical SEO or regular publishing after launch still matters.

q6.question: Do you issue a VAT invoice?
q6.answer: Yes. I operate legally in Poland, I issue an invoice, and you can deduct VAT. A conversation is not a contract — first we check whether we are a good fit.

q7.question: Do you work with clients in Warsaw?
q7.answer: Yes. I work from Poznań, and with Warsaw clients remotely and in person when I am in the city. You do not need to travel — the first conversation is online.

commerce.heroTitle: An online store that belongs to you — without platform commission
commerce.heroSubtitle: I build WooCommerce stores from scratch or from what you already sell: products, payments, and ownership of the code. You pay the gateway per transaction, not a marketplace for the right to sell.

whoFor.title: Who is this online store for?
whoFor.intro: I build stores for brands that want to sell on their own domain — from scratch or from what already works. You do not hand margin to Allegro, Shopify, or yet another all-in-one.

item1.title: Physical and digital products
item1.text: Courses, ebooks, merch, parts, paid services. If the customer should pay you, not a third-party platform — this is the service.

item2.title: From scratch or from a marketplace
item2.text: No store yet? I build it from scratch. You already have a site or marketplace sales and want your own checkout? That too. We do not start with a 40-slide omnichannel strategy — we start with a cart that works.

item3.title: Poznań and Warsaw
item3.text: I build the store remotely on your hosting — from Poznań and for Warsaw firms alike. We can meet in person when I am in Warsaw; the rest happens in code, not in an agency office.

problem.title: Why a marketplace or Shopify is not "your store"
problem.p1: Allegro, Amazon, Shopify take a cut or a subscription for access to customers you still have to acquire. The rules change without you. Leaving hurts because the catalogue, reviews, and checkout live with them.
problem.p2: Your own store does three things: it sells on your domain, keeps orders with you, and does not ask a platform for permission when you change the rules. The rest — themes, sliders, "AI recommendations" — is decoration.

process.title: How an online-store project actually works
process.subtitle: No agency theatre. A conversation, a catalogue, implementation, handover.

step1.title: Conversation
step1.description: What you sell, where traffic comes from, which payments, digital, physical, or both. A WooCommerce store — from scratch or from a catalogue you already have. Not "some ecommerce".

step2.title: Catalogue and payments
step2.description: Product structure, rates, gateway, shipping or file delivery. You see the direction before the store goes to production.

step3.title: Implementation
step3.description: Code, cart, mobile version, basic SEO. Status updates along the way. No silence and no kickoff progress bars.

step4.title: Handover
step4.description: Your store, your domain, a guide for adding products. 30 days of care after launch, so I carry the risk that payments die on Friday night.

includesMore.title: What else is included in the online store?
includesMore.item1: Full ownership on WooCommerce — not an account in a website builder. I can build the store from scratch.
includesMore.item2: Payment gateways without a hidden platform subscription. You pay per transaction, not for "being in the ecosystem".
includesMore.item3: A cart and checkout that can be finished on a phone, not only on a laptop.
includesMore.item4: Basic SEO: titles, descriptions, indexing. Google should be able to find the store before anyone "launches ads".
includesMore.item5: Hosting and domain stay on your side. Leaving does not require Shopify's permission.

whyCustom.title: Why not Shoper, Shopify, or a "store for 300 zł"?
whyCustom.p1: A builder is fast until you want to change the rules, the rates, or export customers. Then you pay a subscription and discover the store was never yours. That is vendor lock-in for a shopping cart.
whyCustom.p2: With me you get a store you actually own. WooCommerce on your infrastructure, payments without a platform middleman, and code you can take with you. You are not renting the right to sell.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions about online stores

q1.question: How much does an online store cost?
q1.answer: The package starts at 6000 PLN net. A simple catalogue with payments is a different job than variants, stock, and integrations — after a conversation you get a quote, not empty from-to ranges.

q2.question: WooCommerce or Shopify?
q2.answer: Shopify is convenient until you accept the subscription and the fact that the store lives with them. WooCommerce gives ownership: theme, plugins, database, domain. If you want your own store, we do not build it on someone else's platform.

q3.question: Can I sell digital products?
q3.answer: Yes. WooCommerce with file delivery after payment. A course, an ebook, a licence — no courier, and no 30% to a marketplace.

q4.question: How long does it take to launch a store?
q4.answer: A straightforward store from scratch is usually a few weeks from kickoff to first orders. The timeline depends on the catalogue, photos, VAT rates, and decisions — not on how many customer-journey workshops we run.

q5.question: Will the store show up in Google?

telemedicine.title: Telemedicine platform
telemedicine.subtitle: For clinics and medical brands that want to issue prescriptions and guide patients online.
telemedicine.heroTitle: A telemedicine platform from questionnaire to prescription and pharmacy
telemedicine.heroSubtitle: I design and implement services where the patient follows a clear path — from intake, through a doctor's review, to receiving medication.
telemedicine.feature1: Patient questionnaire and a path to an e-prescription or doctor consultation
telemedicine.feature2: Medical product catalog, payments, and partner-pharmacy fulfillment
telemedicine.feature3: Trust-building design: a clear process, communication, and conversion without extra friction

whoFor.title: Who is a telemedicine platform for?
whoFor.intro: I build services for clinics, e-prescription brands, and medical products that need to take a patient from intake to a decision — not just "have a pretty health website".

item1.title: Clinic and e-prescription
item1.text: The path: questionnaire, clinical review, document, optionally a pharmacy. The patient should know what happens at each step — not guess from icons.

item2.title: A medical brand online
item2.text: Catalogue, payment, fulfillment. When a product without a clear process burns ad budget, the problem is not "not enough leads". The problem is friction on the path.

item3.title: A team that already knows the rules
item3.text: I design and ship the product. The medical model, contracts with doctors and the pharmacy stay on your side. I do not pretend to be a law firm and I do not sell "compliance in the package".

problem.title: Why a calling-card site is not enough in telemedicine
problem.p1: A patient does not buy a slider with a smiling doctor. They buy the sense that someone owns the process: question, decision, document, pickup. If they get lost between "book a visit" and a form, they go back to a competitor or a walk-in pharmacy.
problem.p2: A ready-made medical SaaS can be fast at the start and expensive at scale: fees, limits, no code, terms you do not negotiate. Your own platform is a product you run — not an account they can terminate.

process.title: How a telemedicine platform project actually works
process.subtitle: Patient path first, then code. No "digital health transformation" theatre.

step1.title: Conversation
step1.description: Who the patient is, what they should get (consult, e-prescription, product), who issues the document, where payment and fulfillment go. We draw the path before I open an editor.

step2.title: Process design
step2.description: Questionnaire, states, messages, cart or a fee for the review. You see friction on paper, not after the ad campaign starts.

step3.title: Implementation
step3.description: The service, panels, payments, the integrations you actually need. Status updates along the way. No six weeks of silence.

step4.title: Handover
step4.description: Your platform, your hosting, documentation. Care after launch, because the first real patient always finds a case that was not on the slide.

includesMore.title: What else is included in the telemedicine platform?
includesMore.item1: A questionnaire and intake states — the patient does not send "an email to reception" and wait in a void.
includesMore.item2: A path to an e-prescription or consult, wired to how your doctors actually work — not magic in a plugin.
includesMore.item3: Catalogue, payments, and, if needed, a handoff to a partner pharmacy or delivery.
includesMore.item4: A layout that builds trust: clear language, no extra friction, mobile first, because patients do not fill this at a desk.
includesMore.item5: Code and infrastructure on your side. We do not build a product you cannot take with you.

whyCustom.title: Why not a "for doctors" template or a ready SaaS?
whyCustom.p1: A clinic template looks like a clinic. It does not walk the patient through. Medical SaaS starts fast, then the fee, the intake cap, and no access to your data turn out not to be an "implementation detail".
whyCustom.p2: A dedicated platform costs more at the start because you are buying ownership. Path psychology, integrations you choose, and code that stays with you. Telemedicine without control of the process is just ads that burn budget.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions about telemedicine platforms
faq.subtitle: Straight answers before we book a call.

q1.question: How much does a telemedicine platform cost?
q1.answer: It is an individual quote. A questionnaire plus e-prescription is a different job than a catalogue, payments, and a pharmacy. After a conversation you get a scope and a number, not an empty from-to.

q2.question: Do you handle medical regulatory compliance?
q2.answer: I am not a law firm and I do not sell a certificate. I design and ship the service inside the model you already have or are building with your own doctors, lawyers, and pharmacy. If nobody can issue the document, code will not replace that.

q3.question: How long does implementation take?
q3.answer: It depends on the path, the integrations, and how fast decisions land on your side. A first working slice can be weeks; a full catalogue and fulfillment takes longer. I do not paint a date on a kickoff slide.

q4.question: Can you connect a partner pharmacy and payments?
q4.answer: Yes — if there is someone and something to connect. I build the catalogue, checkout, and order handoff. The pharmacy contract and settlement stay with you. I do not promise a magical "pharmacy network in the package".

q5.question: How is this different from a ready-made SaaS platform?
q5.answer: You rent SaaS. At scale you pay a cut, wait on their roadmap, and you do not leave with your data without pain. Your own platform is more expensive at the start and cheaper when you stop being a "small customer" in someone else's product.

q6.question: Do you issue a VAT invoice?
q6.answer: Yes. I operate legally in Poland, I issue an invoice, and you can deduct VAT. A conversation is not a contract — first we check whether we are a good fit.

dataCollection.title: Data collection (scraping)
dataCollection.subtitle: For companies that need a clean database from public sources — for a CRM, a platform, or sales.
dataCollection.heroTitle: A public-data database, ready to import
dataCollection.heroSubtitle: I collect, clean, and deliver data from public sources in a format you can upload to your platform, CRM, or campaign.
dataCollection.feature1: Collecting records from public sources: registries, directories, listings, and websites
dataCollection.feature2: Cleaning, deduplication, and field mapping to match your system
dataCollection.feature3: Export ready to import — CSV, spreadsheet, API, or a direct upload

whoFor.title: Who is data collection for?
whoFor.intro: I collect public data for companies that need a database for a CRM, a catalogue, or sales — not another spreadsheet nobody wants to open.

item1.title: Sales and CRM
item1.text: Records from registries, directories, listings. So a salesperson does not retype a tax ID from a PDF, but gets a file they can import.

item2.title: Platform and catalogue
item2.text: When your service needs complete cards, prices, or locations from sources that are already public — only nobody wants to collect them by hand every week.

item3.title: A team that does not buy "magic leads"
item3.text: I do not sell a list of 100 thousand "hot Facebook companies". I work on sources you name, or that we agree are public and useful.

problem.title: Why an intern in Excel is not a data strategy
problem.p1: Copy-pasting from a registry looks cheap until you count errors, duplicates, and the month later when nobody remembers which column is the tax ID. A bought "company database" is often stale, legally messy to use, or just junk.
problem.p2: Proper collection does three things: it takes from a public source, cleans to your schema, and delivers a file or an import you can use. The rest — "AI scraping over the weekend" — ends with half the records and a letter from a lawyer.

process.title: How data collection actually works
process.subtitle: Source, collect, clean, deliver. No promise to scrape the whole internet.

step1.title: Sources and fields
step1.description: What we collect, from where, and in what shape it should land with you. We agree what is public and what the database is for — before I write a scraper.

step2.title: Collection
step2.description: Records from the named registries, directories, listings, sites. I respect source limits and rules. I do not break logins and I do not promise "everything behind a paywall".

step3.title: Cleaning
step3.description: Duplicates, empty fields, mapping onto your columns. A database you cannot import is worse than not having one.

step4.title: Delivery
step4.description: CSV, spreadsheet, API, or a direct upload. Field documentation. If it should be recurring, we say so — we do not hide a subscription under "maintenance".

includesMore.title: What else is included in data collection?
includesMore.item1: Collection only from public sources we name together — registries, directories, listings, websites.
includesMore.item2: Deduplication and normalisation so a tax ID, name, and address do not appear in three spellings.
includesMore.item3: Field mapping for a CRM, platform, or campaign — not a raw dump and best wishes.
includesMore.item4: An export you can import: CSV, spreadsheet, API, or an upload we handle together.
includesMore.item5: A clear scope: what is in the database, what is not, when it was collected. No magical completeness.

whyCustom.title: Why not buy a ready-made list or "just run a bot"?
whyCustom.p1: A ready-made list is cheap until you check the date, the legal basis, and whether anyone cleaned it. A tutorial bot dies on an HTML change and leaves you with half a script nobody wants to touch.
whyCustom.p2: With me you pay for a collection that matches your schema and that you can actually import. Public data, scope in writing, a format your CRM will swallow. I do not sell other people's Facebook lists.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions about data collection
faq.subtitle: Straight answers before we book a call.

q1.question: How much does collecting a public-source database cost?
q1.answer: It is an individual quote. It depends on the number of sources, fields, cleaning, and whether this is a one-off dump or a cycle. After a conversation you get a scope and a number, not a "price per record" from nowhere.

q2.question: Is scraping legal?
q2.answer: I work on public sources — registries, directories, sites without breaking a login. That does not waive your GDPR duties for further use (contact, profiling, sales). If the database goes into cold email, the legal basis is on you. I do not collect data from behind a paywall or from private accounts.

q3.question: What format do I get the data in?
q3.answer: CSV, spreadsheet, API, or a direct upload into your system — we decide at the start. I do not hand over raw HTML and call it a deliverable.

q4.question: Will the database still be fresh in a month?
q4.answer: A one-off collection is a snapshot. Sources change. If you need refreshes, we talk about a cycle in the open — I do not pretend a one-off CSV lives forever.

q5.question: How is this different from buying a ready-made lead list?
q5.answer: A ready-made list has someone else's date, quality, and often someone else's legal problem. I collect what you name as public, into your fields. Fewer records, more of them you can import and stand behind.

q6.question: Do you issue a VAT invoice?
q6.answer: Yes. I operate legally in Poland, I issue an invoice, and you can deduct VAT. A conversation is not a contract — first we check whether the sources and the use make sense.

whoFor.title: Who is technical SEO for?
whoFor.intro: I fix the technical layer of sites that "are online" but that Google cannot see, cannot understand, or punishes for errors nobody reads in Search Console.

item1.title: The site exists, Google is silent
item1.text: You have a website, maybe even content, and the queries do not move. Before someone sells you "rankings and links", it is worth checking whether the crawler even enters and indexes.

item2.title: After a redesign or a migration
item2.text: New site, old URLs, vanished traffic. Canonicals, 404s, a sitemap from a previous era. That is not "the algorithm". That is usually an unfinished move.

item3.title: Poznań and Warsaw
item3.text: Audit and fixes on your stack, remotely. Sites in Poznań and Warsaw go through the same process — WordPress, Nuxt, whatever, as long as there is access. You do not need an agency with a 40-person "SEO content" department.

problem.title: Why "SEO" does nothing if Google cannot enter the site
problem.p1: The agency writes copy while robots.txt blocks a folder. Or the page weighs eight megabytes on a phone, canonicals point at the void, and Search Console has been shouting about indexing for six months. That is not a "weak content" problem. It is a technical blocker.
problem.p2: Technical SEO does not promise a ranking for "website Poznań". It gives the search engine a chance: crawl, index, understandable content, speed, structured data. Without that, content and links work in a vacuum.

process.title: How technical SEO actually works
process.subtitle: Audit, plan, fixes, Search Console. No 80-page report nobody reads.

step1.title: Audit
step1.description: Indexing, crawl, Core Web Vitals, sitemap, robots, canonicals, redirects, structured data, Search Console errors. A list of facts, not "recommendations to consider".

step2.title: Plan
step2.description: What blocks hardest, what we touch first, what we leave because it is content or off-site. You see the order and the scope before anyone touches code.

step3.title: Fixes
step3.description: Meta, sitemap, robots, redirects, canonicals, speed, mobile, schema where it helps. Status updates along the way — not silence and not a slide that says "on-page 40%".

step4.title: After
step4.description: Search Console set up, a change report, what to watch. So I do not disappear on the day Google finally starts crawling.

includesMore.title: What else is included in technical SEO?
includesMore.item1: A check that Google can enter, index, and not get lost in duplicates.
includesMore.item2: Sitemap, robots, canonicals, redirects — boring work that decides whether the new site lives.
includesMore.item3: Core Web Vitals and mobile: not "pretty design", but whether a phone can even load the content.
includesMore.item4: Structured data where it helps the engine understand the page — not 15 schema types "because that is what you do".
includesMore.item5: A report: what was broken, what I changed, what technique will not fix (content, links, time).

whyCustom.title: Why not a package of "SEO + 20 articles + links"?
whyCustom.p1: Copy on a site the crawler does not index is a cost. Links into a canonical mess are a cost with interest. First you unblock crawl. Then writing and linking start to make sense.
whyCustom.p2: I do not sell rankings. I sell the layer without which Google cannot find you, or finds a version you did not want. The rest — content, PR, time — you do on purpose, not instead of fixing the sitemap.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions about technical SEO
faq.subtitle: Straight answers before we book a call.

q1.question: How much does technical SEO cost?
q1.answer: It is an individual quote. Auditing a small calling-card site is a different job than a store with a thousand canonical variants. After a conversation and a look at Search Console you get a scope, not a subscription "for rankings".

q2.question: Do you guarantee Google rankings?
q2.answer: No. Nobody honest guarantees queries. I guarantee that I fix what can be fixed technically: indexing, crawl, the errors the tools show. Rankings also take content, links, and time.

q3.question: How is technical SEO different from content SEO?
q3.answer: Technical: can the crawler enter, understand, avoid duplicates, does the site even work on a phone. Content: is there something to read and will anyone link it. Without the first, the second often never starts.

q4.question: Do I need Google Search Console?
q4.answer: Yes, if you want to know what Google actually sees, not guess from a rank tracker. As part of aftercare I set up GSC and show you where to look — I do not leave you with a login and a screenshot.

q5.question: How long do the audit and the fixes take?
q5.answer: The audit itself can be days. Fixes depend on the stack and who implements (me or your team). A migration with hundreds of redirects is not "we will tweak meta on Friday".

q6.question: Do you issue a VAT invoice?
q6.answer: Yes. I operate legally in Poland, I issue an invoice, and you can deduct VAT. A conversation is not a contract — first we check whether the problem is technical, or whether someone sold you rankings blind.

q7.question: Do you do technical SEO for sites in Warsaw?
q7.answer: Yes. Audit and fixes are remote, on your stack. I am based in Poznań; Warsaw sites go through the same process. We can meet in person when I am in the city — it is not required to start.

whoFor.title: Who is Meta Pixel and CAPI for?
whoFor.intro: I configure tracking for companies that already spend on Meta and see the dashboard lie: fewer purchases than the store, leads that never arrived, an algorithm that 'stopped working'.

item1.title: Ads spend, reports shrink
item1.text: The budget is there. ROAS looks worse month after month. Before someone sells you 'creative and a new funnel', it is worth checking whether events even reach Meta — especially from iPhone and from people with an ad blocker.

item2.title: Store or lead form
item2.text: WooCommerce, a custom checkout, a contact form. Pixel in the browser misses part of the path. CAPI sends the same event from the server. Without that pairing, you train the algorithm on leftovers.

item3.title: Poznań and Warsaw
item3.text: Setup on your stack, remotely. Sites in Poznań and Warsaw go through the same process — WordPress, Nuxt, a store, whatever, as long as there is access. You do not need an agency with a 20-person 'performance' department.

problem.title: Why a Pixel in the footer is not a configuration
problem.p1: Safari cuts cookies. iOS asks for tracking and most people say no. An ad blocker swallows the script. The agency ticks 'Pixel installed', and Events Manager shows a red Event Match Quality, duplicates, or silence after a purchase from a phone. That is not 'the algorithm'. That is a hole in the data.
problem.p2: CAPI does not replace Pixel. It is the second channel: the same event, from the server, with a shared event_id so Meta can merge instead of double-count. Without that, you either lose conversions or invent them.

process.title: How a Pixel and CAPI setup actually works
process.subtitle: Audit, event map, implementation, test in Events Manager. No 'we will add a Pixel on Friday'.

step1.title: Audit
step1.description: What Pixel is already there, which events fire, whether CAPI exists, whether event_id matches, what EMQ looks like, whether consent is respected. A list of facts, not a screenshot from GTM.

step2.title: Map
step2.description: Which events the campaign needs (Lead is not Purchase), which parameters, which user data we hash and when we do not send them. You see the scope before anyone touches code.

step3.title: Implementation
step3.description: Pixel, CAPI, deduplication, tests in Events Manager. Status updates along the way — not silence and not a slide that says 'tracking 80%'.

step4.title: Handover
step4.description: What is firing, where to look, what to watch after a campaign change. So I do not disappear on the day Meta finally starts seeing purchases.

includesMore.title: What else is included in Pixel and CAPI?
includesMore.item1: A check of existing Pixel / GTM / plugin — I do not stack a second Pixel 'just in case'.
includesMore.item2: event_id on the browser and the server, so Meta merges instead of duplicating.
includesMore.item3: Hashed matching parameters (email, phone) where consent allows — EMQ is not a decoration.
includesMore.item4: A consent-aware setup: no sending everything 'because the ads need it'. GDPR is not a slogan in the footer.
includesMore.item5: A report: what was firing, what I changed, what tracking will not fix (offer, creative, budget).

whyCustom.title: Why not a WordPress plugin and 'CAPI in one click'?
whyCustom.p1: A plugin often sends something. Rarely the right thing: a shared event_id, the right parameters, without duplicates, with consent. 'One click' is a slogan. The result is a Pixel that fires Purchase on the cart and CAPI that fires it again at thank-you.
whyCustom.p2: I do not sell 'higher ROAS'. I sell the layer without which Meta cannot learn, or learns from noise. Creative, budget, and offer stay on your side — on purpose, not instead of fixing events.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions about Meta Pixel and CAPI
faq.subtitle: Straight answers before we book a call.

q1.question: How much does Pixel and CAPI setup cost?
q1.answer: The package starts at 1000 PLN net. A Pixel on a calling-card site with a form is a different job than a store with a checkout, upsells, and three thank-you pages — after a conversation you get a quote, not a subscription 'for better ads'.

q2.question: What is the difference between Pixel and CAPI?
q2.answer: Pixel runs in the browser and is easy to block. CAPI sends the same events from the server. Together, with a shared event_id, they give Meta a fuller picture without double-counting. Pixel alone is a guess. CAPI alone without Pixel is also incomplete — Meta expects both.

q3.question: Is a WooCommerce or WordPress plugin enough?
q3.answer: Sometimes as a starting point. Rarely as a finished setup. Plugins duplicate events, skip event_id, send Purchase too early, or ignore consent. I check what is already there and fix it — I do not install a second plugin on top of the first.

q4.question: What about GDPR and cookie consent?
q4.answer: Events with personal data go out when there is a basis to send them. I do not 'turn consent off so ads work better'. Pixel and CAPI can be set to respect the banner. If the current setup sends everything to everyone, that is a problem, not a feature.

q5.question: How long does configuration take?
q5.answer: A simple form-plus-Pixel can be days. A store with a custom checkout, several events, and an existing GTM mess is longer. The timeline depends on access (site, Events Manager, hosting) — not on how many slides I show at kickoff.

q6.question: Do you issue a VAT invoice?
q6.answer: Yes. I operate legally in Poland, I issue an invoice, and you can deduct VAT. A conversation is not a contract — first we check whether the problem is tracking, or whether someone sold you ads on a Pixel that never fired.

q7.question: Do you configure Pixel and CAPI for sites in Warsaw?
q7.answer: Yes. The work is remote, on your stack. I am based in Poznań; Warsaw sites go through the same process. We can meet in person when I am in the city — it is not required to start.
